Compliance · Kenya

Kenya drone law: what a commercial aerial survey needs

Kenya’s drone rules were rewritten in the Civil Aviation (Unmanned Aircraft Systems) Regulations, 2025 (Legal Notice No. 40 of 2026, published on 6 March 2026). Anyone flying for reward needs an RPAS Operator Certificate from the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, and KCAA issues it only to a company registered and based in Kenya that has a security clearance from the Ministry responsible for defence. Each operation also needs KCAA authorisation, and aerial photography for mapping needs a month’s written notice to the Director of Surveys. This page summarises the public rules as last reviewed on 27 September 2026, with the source for each; it is not legal advice.

As of 27 September 2026

This page summarises public rules for information. It is not legal advice.

Request a proposal Checklist for clients

At a glance

Six things a commercial drone job needs

The company, its people, each drone, each flight, the survey authority and the site each have their own approval. A commercial drone job is lawful only when all of them are in place for that area and that date.

KCAA, regs 24–29

An RPAS Operator Certificate

Required for “commercial activities, reward or hire”, with operations specifications attached. Issued only to a company registered in Kenya with its principal place of business there, and valid for 24 months.

Regs 4 and 26(d)

Security clearances

A clearance from the relevant Government Security Agency for anyone who intends to engage in UAS operations, valid for 24 months, and a security clearance from the Ministry responsible for defence as a condition of the operator certificate.

KCAA, regs 23 and 36

Authorisation of each operation

No operation “without authorization as prescribed by the Authority”, with the dates, route, levels, payload, insurance and security compliance set out in the request.

Regs 8, 11 and 30

Registered drones and pilot licences

Each drone imported under a KCAA permit and registered, with its identification displayed at all times, and a KCAA remote pilot licence for the pilot in command and co-pilot in categories B and C.

Survey Act, s.42

Notice to the Director of Surveys

At least one month’s written notice before “any aerial photography for use in mapping or similar purpose”, with photographs produced for inspection on request.

Owners and officers in charge

Site permissions

The asset owner’s and landowners’ permission for take-off and landing sites, and written authority before imaging any prohibited or protected place.

Before anything else

Which rules apply: confirm it with KCAA

The 2025 Regulations are published, but Legal Notice 40 neither revokes the 2020 ones nor says when it commences.

The Civil Aviation (Unmanned Aircraft Systems) Regulations, 2025 were made on 15 December 2025 by the Cabinet Secretary for Transport and Roads under section 82 of the Civil Aviation Act (Cap. 394), and published as Legal Notice No. 40 of 2026 in Kenya Gazette Supplement No. 50 of 6 March 2026. They are one of 36 revised regulations KCAA uploaded in its notice on the Kenya Civil Aviation Regulations, alongside the Civil Aviation (Security) Regulations, 2025 (Legal Notice No. 31 of 2026) and the Civil Aviation (Aerial Work – General Operations) Regulations, 2025 (Legal Notice No. 44 of 2026).

Three things are not settled on the face of the documents:

  • Commencement and revocation. Legal Notice 40 has no commencement clause and no revocation clause, and KCAA’s drone page still offered the 2020 Regulations (Legal Notice No. 42 of 2020), the 2020 Manual of Implementing Standards and the 2021 fees as its downloads on 27 September 2026.
  • The security regulations named in the text. Regulation 4(4) refers to “The Civil Aviation Security Regulation 2024” for national security vetting; the regulations actually published are the Security Regulations, 2025.
  • Aerial work. The Aerial Work Regulations define “aerial survey” to include imagery collected by UAVs (reg 2) and require authorisation when it is done for business or hire (reg 51). Their pilot rules are written for manned aircraft, so whether they apply to drone surveys is a question to put to KCAA.

Ask in writing

Before a drone job is costed or scheduled, ask KCAA or your counsel to confirm:

  • which UAS Regulations KCAA applies to the operation;
  • whether the Aerial Work Regulations’ authorisation applies to it;
  • which fee schedule applies.

KCAA’s online services run through its RPAS Operations Management System.

The layers

Who authorises what

Layer Body Instrument What it controls
Airspace, safety, drones and operators Kenya Civil Aviation Authority UAS Regulations 2025 (LN 40/2026) Registration, import and export permits, operation authorisations, the RPAS Operator Certificate, remote pilot licences, training organisations, resellers, security programmes
National security vetting The relevant Government Security Agency Reg 4 A clearance for any person who intends to engage in UAS operations, valid for 24 months; approvals can be amended, suspended or revoked on security findings (4(3))
Defence clearance The Ministry responsible for defence Reg 26(d) A condition of every operator certificate; KCAA seeks it “in the course of processing the application”
Aerial photography for mapping Director of Surveys Survey Act (Cap. 299), s.42 One month’s written notice; photographs produced for inspection, and copies supplied at the Director’s cost, on written request; copyright unaffected
Radio equipment Communications Authority of Kenya Kenya Information and Communications Act (Cap. 411A) Type approval of command-and-control and video links
Prohibited places The officer in charge, or the Minister Official Secrets Act (Cap. 187), ss.2–3 An offence to photograph a prohibited place, or in one, without the authority of the officer in charge
Protected areas The Minister, by Gazette Protected Areas Act (Cap. 204), ss.3–4 No entry without permission
National-security no-fly areas KCAA Reg 45(3) A Gazette notice can prohibit drones “in any specific area in Kenya for any period in the interest of national security”
Personal data Office of the Data Protection Commissioner Data Protection Act 2019; reg 60(5) Images of people are personal data; “property details” are sensitive personal data (DPA s.2)

The operator

The RPAS Operator Certificate

When it is needed. For “commercial activities, reward or hire” (reg 24(1)), with operations specifications attached that set out what the operator may do. The company names an Accountable Executive and heads of operations, maintenance, quality and safety, and runs a safety management system.

Who can get one. KCAA “may issue” the certificate to an applicant that (reg 26):

  • (a) “has its principal place of business and it is registered in Kenya”;
  • (b) meets the standards;
  • (c) is qualified, staffed and equipped;
  • (d) has “a security clearance issued by the Ministry responsible for matters relating to defence”;
  • (e) has an acceptable aircraft operator security programme.

Timing and validity. Apply at least 90 days before the intended operation (reg 25(2)). The certificate is valid for 24 months from issue or renewal (reg 27), and an expired certificate needs a new initial application (reg 27(3)). Under the 2020 Manual of Implementing Standards, the process runs in five phases: a pre-application statement of intent after government-agency clearance, the formal application (operations manual, safety management system, quality and security manuals), document evaluation, a demonstration, and certification.

What the public list shows. KCAA publishes a list of operator certificates in a PDF created on 8 January 2024. It says nothing about any company’s status today: ask for the certificate itself.

Duties that come with the certificate

  • A security programme approved by KCAA (reg 62).
  • Vetting (reg 63): background checks on everyone recruited to deploy, handle or store drones, criminal-record checks every 24 months, secure storage protected against tampering, a named security coordinator and staff training.
  • Loss or theft reported to the relevant Government Security Agencies and KCAA (reg 44).
  • Records kept “with all data protection laws of Kenya” (reg 58(3)).
  • Insurance: third-party cover in force, with the certificate kept at operational management (reg 59).
  • Contractors that KCAA has not certificated follow the operator’s approved safety and security procedures, and KCAA may inspect them (reg 37).

Security

Two clearances, and the places they protect

Clearance for people. Anyone who “intends to engage in UAS operations” needs a security clearance as prescribed by KCAA, valid for 24 months (reg 4). Approvals can be amended, suspended or revoked on security findings.

Clearance for the operator. Every operator certificate needs a security clearance from the Ministry responsible for defence (reg 26(d)). The 2020 Manual lists a security clearance “already received in pre-application phase” among the documents for the formal application (§5.3.1(f)).

Interference and interception. Unlawful interference with an authorised operation is an offence (reg 66). KCAA may intercept or take control of a drone where there is a contravention, a serious and imminent risk, or a threat to national security (reg 67), and may seize drones (reg 18).

Near military sites

Security restrictions around military installations shape infrastructure itself: part of a recent 132 kV line was put underground “because of security restrictions around Laikipia Air Base” (Capital FM, 28 August 2026). Plan on no drone flight near a military installation without the defence authorities’ agreement.

Each drone and each pilot

Ownership, import, registration and licences

Reg 7

Who may own a drone

A Kenyan citizen or resident aged 18 or over; a body corporate “lawfully recognized and doing business under the laws of Kenya”, including UN bodies and NGOs; national or county government; and bodies corporate of other countries the Authority may approve. Military-specification drones need KCAA approval (reg 7(3)).

Regs 8 and 10

Import and sale

A KCAA permit to import or export, processed “in conjunction with relevant government agencies” (Manual §1.3). Drones are sold only as the Authority prescribes, and KCAA lists the resellers it has approved.

Reg 11

Registration

A certificate of registration, with the identification displayed “at all times”. Drones under an operator certificate show the manufacturer’s serial number or the KCAA mark. Drones already imported must be registered within six months of commencement (reg 167).

Communications Authority

Radios

Command-and-control and video links need type approval from the Communications Authority of Kenya.

Regs 30 and 32

Remote pilots

A KCAA remote pilot licence for the pilot in command and the co-pilot in categories B and C; category A skills “as prescribed”. Training only at an RPAS Training Organisation KCAA has certificated.

Reg 6

Categories

A (open, low risk), B (specific, medium risk) and C, the certification category (high risk, where Part B also applies). The text sets no weight or distance thresholds; KCAA “may from time to time determine additional requirements” (reg 6(2)).

Under the Manual (§1.2), applicants open an online account; individuals submit their ID and a police clearance certificate issued within the last year, and companies their registration documents.

Each flight

Authorisation of every operation

No operation may take place “without authorization as prescribed by the Authority” (reg 23). Drones registered abroad need authorisation too (reg 23(2)), and operations are authorised by category (reg 23(3)–(4)). The request covers (reg 36(2)):

  • the operator and the aircraft, with copies of the registration, the operator certificate and the pilot licences;
  • the radio station licence;
  • the intended operation: dates, route, levels and duration;
  • performance, command-and-control links, detect-and-avoid and emergency procedures;
  • “confirmation of compliance with the Civil Aviation (Security) Regulations”;
  • the payload;
  • “proof of adequate insurance coverage”.

Documents not in English need an English translation and a certificate of translation (reg 36(4)).

What this means for a corridor

A long line crosses several counties, landowners and, often, aerodrome zones and high-tension lines. Each of those can add a permission to the authorisation. Satellite screening first narrows the flying to the stretches where drone detail is worth it.

Satellite first, drones where they add detail

The flight

Operating limits that shape a corridor survey

The 2025 text, unless stated. KCAA may approve more than the defaults; none of them can be waived by the client.

Rule What the 2025 Regulations say
Height and distance Not “above 400 feet Above Ground Level (AGL) and within 30 meters of any person, vessel, vehicle or structure which is not under the control of the person in charge” (reg 38(1)(a)); KCAA may approve more (38(2)). The 2020 Regulations and Manual said 50 m. The text joins the two limits with “and”: ask counsel how KCAA applies them.
Sensor footprint No operation “where cameras, imaging devices or other sensors capture information, pictures or videos extending beyond the prescribed area of approved operation” (reg 38(1)(c))
Weather Visual meteorological conditions only, unless the pilot is rated and the system approved (reg 38(1)(b) and (3))
Congested areas At least 30 m lateral from any person, building, structure, vehicle, vessel or animal not associated with the operation, unless authorised (reg 47)
Public roads Not over, or less than 30 m along, a public road unless reasonable care is taken for road users (reg 48); no take-off or landing on a public road without approval, except in an emergency (reg 49)
Aerodromes Not within 10 km of the aerodrome reference point of a category C–F aerodrome, or 7 km of a category A–B aerodrome, nor on approach and take-off paths, near navigation aids, in the aerodrome traffic zone or in holding patterns, without the written permission of the aerodrome operator and the air navigation service provider plus KCAA approval (reg 56)
Controlled airspace Flight plans as prescribed (reg 52), with air traffic control made aware (reg 55)
Night Within visual or extended visual line of sight, and only if expressly authorised (reg 39)
Beyond visual line of sight Only “as prescribed by the Authority” (reg 40); autonomous and highly automated drones likewise (regs 41–42)
Loss of control link Reported to KCAA immediately (reg 54(2))
Insurance Third-party cover in force, with the minimum sum notified to KCAA; KCAA may dispense with it by category (reg 59)

Beyond line of sight in practice

KCAA approved the Konza National Drone Corridor, initiated by the Konza Technopolis Development Authority, after review by its UAS Multi-Agency Route Committee: “Kenya’s first controlled airspace specifically dedicated to Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) drone operations” (KBC, 8 July 2025). KCAA has also published route-specific procedures for autonomous flights in class G airspace in western Kenya, with radio licences, route approvals and higher minimum heights for helicopters inside the approved route areas. A new beyond-line-of-sight corridor is a bespoke multi-agency approval with no published timeline, so pipeline and power-line jobs are planned as blocks flown within visual or extended visual line of sight.

Sensitive sites

High-tension lines, installations, airports and protected places

Reg 45(2)(c)

High-tension lines and strategic installations

Operating “in or around strategic installations, Air Navigation Service facilities, high tension cables and communication masts, prisons, police stations, courts of law, scenes of crime, schools and hospitals”, except under the conditions or with KCAA’s permission, is deemed negligent or reckless operation. So every drone survey of a transmission line needs specific KCAA permission, plus the utility’s own safety clearances. No public list of “strategic installations” was found; ask KCAA about pipeline stations, depots and terminals before planning.

Reg 45(2)(b) and (3)

Published restricted areas

Flying in the prohibited, restricted and danger areas published in the Aeronautical Information Publication is negligent or reckless unless done under its conditions or with KCAA’s permission. KCAA can also ban drones from a specific area by Gazette notice in the interest of national security, so check the Gazette before each job.

Official Secrets Act, ss.2–3

Prohibited places

“Prohibited place” includes government places used for public security, among them “factories, dockyards, mines… telegraph, telephone, wireless or signal stations”, and places the Minister declares by order. Photographing a prohibited place, or in one, without the authority of the officer in charge is an offence (s.3(2)).

Permissions

Mining sites and private land

There is no drone-specific rule for mines. The licence holder and the landowner give permission for access, and the Aerial Work Regulations expect “a statement that permission has been obtained from property owners or local officials” in a plan for a congested area or controlled airspace (LN 44/2026, reg 54), if KCAA confirms those rules apply to drones.

Data and images

What the camera may capture, and what may be done with it

Stay inside the approved area. Operating where the sensors capture information “extending beyond the prescribed area of approved operation” is itself a breach of the operating limits (reg 38(1)(c)), and such material “shall not be reproduced, processed, shared, distributed or published” (reg 38(4)). Flight lines and the sensor footprint are planned inside the approved polygon, and orthophotos are cropped to it before processing as a second safeguard.

People and private property (reg 60):

  • no image of a person without that person’s written consent;
  • no imaging of private property or its occupants with the intent of watching them, in violation of a reasonable expectation of privacy;
  • “with the approval of the Authority”, an imaging drone may be used for “mapping and evaluating the earth’s surface, including terrain and surface water bodies and other features”, for forest, vegetation and wildlife work and for search and rescue (60(4));
  • other privacy and data laws apply (60(5)), and no nuisance (60(6)).

The Data Protection Act 2019 applies to controllers and processors “not established or ordinarily resident in Kenya, but processing personal data of data subjects located in Kenya” (s.4(b)(ii)), and lists “property details” among sensitive personal data (s.2). See data protection and aerial mapping.

The Survey Act. The Director of Surveys may ask for the photographs to be produced for inspection, and for copies at the Director’s cost (s.42).

Installations. Drone imagery of pipeline, power, military or airport installations is never published: the Official Secrets Act makes photographing a prohibited place without the authority of the officer in charge an offence. Survey imagery goes only to the client’s named contacts.

Enforcement

Penalties and other consequences

The Regulations sort their provisions into two penalty classes (reg 165 and its Schedule):

  • “B” provisions carry a fine or imprisonment of up to three years for each offence. They include categorisation (6), import and export (8), sale (10), operation authorisation (23), the operator certificate (24), the operating limits (38), night (39), prohibited operation (45), congested areas (47), aerodromes (56), privacy (60) and interference (66).
  • “A” provisions carry a fine or imprisonment of up to one year. They include eligibility (7), registration (11), the pilot licence (30), training (32), incident reporting (43), flight plans (52), command and control (54), records (58) and insurance (59).
  • Failing to comply with a KCAA direction, and contraventions with no penalty of their own, are punished like “B” provisions (165(1) and (5)).

Joint liability. The operator and the pilot are both deemed to have contravened a provision unless each proves lack of consent or connivance and due diligence (reg 165(4)).

Other consequences. Suspension or revocation of approvals (reg 163), seizure of drones (reg 18), and appeal to the Tribunal within 21 days (reg 164).

Outside the Regulations. A fine under the Survey Act for failing to give the Director of Surveys notice (s.42), and the offences in the Official Secrets Act.

The fine amounts are set in regulation 165; see the Sources below.

For clients

Checklist: before you commission a drone survey in Kenya

Ask any operator, including one we propose, for each of these before the first flight.

  1. A current KCAA RPAS Operator Certificate

    The number, the 24-month expiry, and operations specifications covering what the job needs: category B or C, night, extended or beyond visual line of sight, congested areas (reg 24). Ask for the certificate itself; the public list of January 2024 proves nothing about current status.

  2. Kenyan registration and principal place of business

    As reg 26(a) requires; for a foreign firm, KCAA’s written recognition of its certificate under reg 35.

  3. Security clearances

    The defence clearance (reg 26(d)) and the personnel clearances (reg 4, 24 months), an approved security programme and a named security coordinator (regs 62–63).

  4. Each drone registered and marked

    Imported under a KCAA permit, registered and marked, with radios type-approved by the Communications Authority.

  5. Remote pilot licences

    KCAA remote pilot licences (reg 30) with the ratings the task needs.

  6. An operation authorisation for this job and this area

    Including KCAA permission for high-tension lines, strategic installations or published restricted areas (reg 45); the aerodrome operator’s, the air navigation service provider’s and KCAA’s permission within 10 km or 7 km of an airfield (reg 56); and approval to use the imaging device for mapping (reg 60(4)).

  7. Notice to the Director of Surveys

    A dated letter giving at least one month’s written notice before the aerial photography (Survey Act s.42).

  8. Aerial-work authorisation, if KCAA says it applies

    The authorisation for aerial survey for business or hire in the Aerial Work Regulations (LN 44/2026, regs 51 and 54), if KCAA confirms that it applies to drones.

  9. Permissions on the ground

    From the asset owner and the landowners for take-off and landing sites; county and security coordination; written authority before imaging any prohibited or protected place (Official Secrets Act s.3(2); Protected Areas Act).

  10. Insurance

    Third-party liability cover naming the project (reg 59).

  11. A data clause

    Flight lines and sensor footprint inside the approved polygon, and nothing outside it kept or shared (reg 38(1)(c) and (4)); people blurred or not captured (reg 60); processing and transfer under the Data Protection Act; who may publish the imagery.

  12. Safety management and site procedures

    The safety management system, a site risk assessment, and emergency and contingency procedures (regs 29 and 53).

  13. Only where field work is safe

    No field or drone work in Mandera, Wajir and Garissa counties, Lamu County outside Lamu and Manda islands, Tana River County, the Kilifi coast north of Malindi, the Turkana and Marsabit border areas, or West Pokot and western Turkana, where government travel advice warns against travel (FCDO, Canada, US, Australia); and a written security plan for field work in the North Rift, where security operations were being expanded to Samburu and Isiolo in September 2026 (Capital FM, 27 September 2026).

How we work

AfriScan and drone work in Kenya

AfriScan screens corridors from satellite imagery. A satellite register needs no aircraft and no flight authorisation, so it can cover a whole wayleave, including in the areas where government travel advice warns against travel, before anyone decides whether a drone is worth sending.

Where drone detail is needed, the flights are carried out by a company registered in Kenya with a current KCAA RPAS Operator Certificate, under that company’s certificate and subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires. Every AfriScan proposal with a drone element names that company and the approvals its flights need, so your team can check them against this page.

Last reviewed: 27 September 2026. This page summarises public rules for information. It is not legal advice. Drone surveys are subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires. Satellite-based work involves no drone flight.

Frequently asked questions

Does a satellite corridor scan need KCAA authorisation?

No aircraft is flown, and the UAS Regulations govern aircraft, so they do not reach the satellite work itself. The Survey Act’s one-month notice speaks of “aerial photography for use in mapping”, which satellite imagery arguably is not; if your project depends on that point, ask counsel to confirm it.

Which rules apply today, the 2020 Regulations or the 2025 ones?

Ask KCAA to confirm in writing. Legal Notice 40 of 2026 has no commencement clause and no clause revoking the 2020 Regulations, and on 27 September 2026 KCAA’s drone page still offered the 2020 Regulations, the 2020 Manual of Implementing Standards and the 2021 fees as its downloads. This page follows the 2025 text and notes where the 2020 rules differed.

Can a foreign company fly commercial drone surveys in Kenya?

Not with a Kenyan operator certificate of its own, which goes only to a company registered in Kenya with its principal place of business there (reg 26(a)). The Regulations let KCAA recognise a certificate issued by another Contracting State whose requirements are at least equal to the applicable standards (reg 35), but how that works for commercial aerial survey has not been tested in the sources we checked, and the 30-day temporary permit for foreign operators in the 2020 Regulations is not in the 2025 text. Plan commercial survey flights with a company that has a Kenyan certificate.

Can a drone survey a transmission line?

Only with KCAA’s specific permission. Operating in or around high-tension cables, communication masts or strategic installations without it is treated as negligent or reckless operation (reg 45(2)(c)). The utility’s own safety clearances come on top.

How far ahead does drone work need to be planned?

A new operator certificate is applied for at least 90 days before the intended operation (reg 25(2)), and the Director of Surveys needs at least one month’s written notice before aerial photography for mapping (Survey Act s.42). With a current certificate in place, the job authorisation, the site permissions and any clearances set the timetable. Satellite work can start while they are arranged.

Can the imagery show people?

An image of a person needs that person’s written consent (reg 60), so a drone survey is planned to avoid capturing people and anyone captured is blurred or left out. Structure registers carry no names.

Is there a corridor where drones can fly beyond line of sight?

KCAA approved the Konza National Drone Corridor as Kenya’s first controlled airspace dedicated to beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations, after review by a multi-agency route committee (KBC, 8 July 2025). Elsewhere, beyond-line-of-sight flying is allowed only as KCAA prescribes (reg 40), so long corridors are planned as blocks flown within visual or extended visual line of sight.

Start from satellite, add drones only where they earn their place.

Send the route or site file and tell us which stretches you want flown. We reply with a satellite scope, a drone plan that names the Kenyan company that will fly and the approvals each flight needs, and a written proposal.
